0. Orientation & Exam Strategy
HPSC Food Safety Officer (Group-B) Master Study Handout
Module: Modern Food Packaging Technology, Migration Regulations & Instrumental Food Analysis

Prepared in the voice of a Senior Professor of Food Packaging Technology and Instrumental Analytical Chemistry, acting as Chief Paper Setter. Every section is written from first principles (polymer physics, material chemistry, spectroscopy, chromatography), then anchored to the statutory number (limit, schedule, prohibition), and finally converted into the examination deliverable (trap box, count-based pair, descriptive skeleton).
How the HPSC pattern rewards you

rows: MCQs, 0.25 negative marking per wrong answer

Precision recall of numbers, names of schedules, polymer properties, detector selectivity; heavy use of "how many of the following statements are correct" (count-based pairs) and absolute qualifiers (always, never, only, all, none)
Structured answer writing: definition, mechanism, labelled schematic, comparative table, statutory citation, conclusion

blocks.text: Rules of engagement for Stage 1

Never answer a count-based pair by instinct. Write c1, c2, c3 in the margin for each statement (1 if correct, 0 if wrong), then compute N = c1 + c2 + c3 and match it to the option. This single discipline removes the majority of negative-marking losses.

Treat every absolute qualifier as a red flag. "EVOH is always the best barrier" is wrong because EVOH fails at high humidity. "Recycled plastics are completely banned" is wrong after the FSSAI certified food-grade recycled PET exception.

Distinguish look-alike pairs on sight: PVC versus PVDC, LDPE versus LLDPE, FAAS versus GFAAS, ECD versus FID, C-enamel versus R-enamel, overall migration versus specific migration, active versus intelligent packaging, time-temperature indicator versus freshness indicator.
Rules of engagement for Stage 2
Open with a one-line definition or statutory citation (regulation name, year, schedule).
Give a mechanism (what happens at the molecular or instrumental level) before giving the application.
Add one labelled schematic (described in words if you cannot draw) and one comparative table; examiners award marks for structure.
Close with a regulatory or public-health linkage, since the post is Food Safety Officer, not Food Technologist.

4.1.6 Remaining HPLC notes: separation science you must be able to write

Reversed-phase versus normal-phase: in reversed-phase HPLC the stationary phase is non-polar (octadecylsilane, C18, bonded to 3 to 5 µm silica) and the mobile phase is polar (water with methanol or acetonitrile, often buffered); polar analytes elute first, and increasing the organic fraction shortens retention. Normal-phase HPLC uses bare silica or amino-bonded silica with a non-polar mobile phase (hexane with isopropanol); non-polar analytes elute first. About 80 percent of food methods are reversed-phase.

Isocratic versus gradient elution: isocratic keeps mobile-phase composition constant (simple, compatible with the refractive index detector); gradient elution raises the organic fraction during the run to elute strongly retained compounds with sharp peaks (required for mixed vitamin or multi-colour screens, incompatible with the refractive index detector because the baseline drifts with composition).

Column efficiency: the van Deemter equation H = A + B/u + C·u relates plate height H to linear velocity u; A is eddy diffusion (particle size and packing), B is longitudinal diffusion, C is resistance to mass transfer. Smaller particles reduce A and C, which is why ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC) uses sub-2 µm particles at pressures up to 1000 to 1500 bar to give ten times faster runs with higher resolution.

Guard columns protect the analytical column from matrix; in-line degassing prevents pump cavitation; sample clean-up uses solid-phase extraction (C18 or immunoaffinity cartridges for aflatoxins) and syringe filtration at 0.45 µm.

blocks.text: 4.1.7 Core HPLC applications in FSSAI enforcement

Vitamins: fat-soluble vitamins A (retinol, 325 nm), D (265 nm), E (tocopherols, 292 nm UV or fluorescence) and K after saponification and hexane extraction, reversed-phase C18 with methanol; water-soluble vitamins (B1, B2, B3, B6, B9, C) by ion-pair reversed-phase with UV or fluorescence detection; vitamin C by reversed-phase on a C18 column at 245 nm with metaphosphoric acid stabilisation. Needed to verify fortification claims (FSS (Fortification of Foods) Regulations, 2018, for example vitamin A and D in edible oil and milk, iron, folic acid and B12 in wheat flour and rice).

Synthetic food colours: extraction of the dye on wool or on a polyamide or C18 solid-phase cartridge, reversed-phase gradient with ammonium acetate buffer and methanol, PDA detection. India permits only eight synthetic colours (tartrazine, sunset yellow FCF, carmoisine, ponceau 4R, erythrosine, indigo carmine, brilliant blue FCF, fast green FCF) at a maximum of 100 mg/kg singly or in combination (200 mg/kg in a few categories), so the method must separate and identify non-permitted dyes such as metanil yellow, rhodamine B, orange II, auramine and Sudan dyes, which are a prosecutable offence.

Aflatoxins B1, B2, G1 and G2: extraction with methanol-water, immunoaffinity column clean-up, reversed-phase C18 with water-methanol-acetonitrile, fluorescence detection. Aflatoxins B1 and G1 fluoresce weakly in aqueous mobile phases, so post-column derivatisation is applied: electrochemically generated bromine (Kobra cell), iodine solution added by a second pump, trifluoroacetic acid pre-column, or a photochemical reactor (UV lamp) that hydrates the terminal furan double bond into the strongly fluorescent hemiacetal. FSSAI limits (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations, 2011, as amended): total aflatoxins 15 µg/kg and aflatoxin B1 10 µg/kg in cereals, nuts and oilseeds, 30 µg/kg total in certain spices such as chillies and nutmeg, and aflatoxin M1 0.5 µg/kg in milk.

Sugar profiling: aminopropyl (NH2) column, acetonitrile-water 75:25 isocratic, refractive index detection; separation order fructose, glucose, sucrose, maltose, lactose; used to detect added sucrose in honey and fruit juices and to verify sugar-free claims. High-performance anion-exchange chromatography with pulsed amperometric detection gives higher sensitivity.

Other routine targets: preservatives (benzoate, sorbate, propionate), artificial sweeteners (saccharin, aspartame, acesulfame-K, sucralose by ELSD), caffeine in energy drinks (FSSAI ceiling 300 mg/L), melamine screening, polyphenols and curcumin content in turmeric, capsaicin in chilli, patulin in apple juice (50 µg/kg limit).

HPSC EXAM TRAP: detector matching
Refractive index detection is universal but insensitive and cannot be used with gradient elution; fluorescence is the most sensitive but only for fluorescent molecules or their derivatives; the photodiode array is the detector that confirms identity by spectrum. Aflatoxins are measured by fluorescence after post-column derivatisation, not by refractive index; sugars are measured by refractive index, not by UV (they have no chromophore).
Part 1. Packaging Materials & Barrier Properties
PART 1: FOOD PACKAGING MATERIALS AND BARRIER PROPERTIES
1.0 Why packaging exists: the four functions
Containment: holding the product in a defined unit.
Protection: against physical (shock, compression), chemical (oxygen, moisture, light, odour) and biological (microbes, insects, rodents) hazards; this is where barrier science lives.
Convenience: portioning, opening, reclosing, microwaveability, retortability.
Communication: labelling, traceability, tamper evidence; this is where the Food Safety Officer meets the Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020.
1.1 Barrier science from first principles
A polymer film is not a wall; it is a solvent. Gas or vapour transport follows the solution-diffusion model:
The permeant dissolves in the polymer surface (governed by the solubility coefficient S).
It diffuses down a concentration gradient (governed by the diffusion coefficient D).
It desorbs on the other side.

Permeability coefficient P = D × S, and the steady-state transmission rate is proportional to P × area × partial-pressure difference divided by thickness. Everything in packaging barrier design manipulates D or S.

blocks.text: Standard units and test methods:
WVTR (water vapour transmission rate): g/m²·day at 38 °C and 90 percent RH (ASTM E96 gravimetric cup; ASTM F1249 infrared sensor).

OTR (oxygen transmission rate): cm³/m²·day·atm at 23 °C, usually 0 or 50 percent RH (ASTM D3985 coulometric sensor). EVOH must always be quoted with its RH because its OTR can rise ten to a hundred fold at 90 percent RH.

HPSC EXAM TRAP: the barrier paradox
No single homopolymer is excellent against both oxygen and water. Polyolefins (PE, PP) are good moisture barriers and poor oxygen barriers; EVOH and nylon are the reverse. PVDC is the only common polymer that is good against both, and aluminium foil is the only material that is essentially total against both plus light. Any statement that EVOH or nylon is a "good moisture barrier" is wrong.
1.2 Glass
Composition (soda-lime-silica container glass)

blocks.text: Properties

Chemical inertness: attacked only by hydrofluoric acid and hot concentrated alkali; no migration of organic substances, which is why glass is the reference inert material. Minor alkali (sodium) leaching into acidic or pharmaceutical products is controlled by hydrolytic resistance classes.
Absolute barrier to gases, vapours, micro-organisms and odours; transparent (consumer appeal but light sensitivity); rigid, stackable, reclosable, microwave compatible, fully recyclable.
Drawbacks: heavy (density about 2.5 g/cm³), brittle, fracture hazard (glass fragments are a critical physical hazard in HACCP plans), poor thermal shock resistance.
Thermal shock resistance

Glass fails under sudden temperature change because the outer surface contracts or expands before the interior, generating tensile stress. Soda-lime container glass survives a sudden differential of only about 40 to 50 °C (hot filling into a cold jar, or cold water on a hot jar, is a classic breakage cause), which is why hot-fill lines pre-warm containers and retort processes raise and lower temperature gradually. Borosilicate glass (about 12 percent B2O3; laboratory and ovenware) has a coefficient of thermal expansion of about 3.3 × 10^-6 per kelvin versus about 9 × 10^-6 for soda-lime glass, so it tolerates differentials well above 100 °C.
Annealing

After forming (blow-and-blow for narrow-neck bottles, press-and-blow for jars on the IS machine) the container cools unevenly and locks in internal stresses. It passes through an annealing lehr held at about 550 to 600 °C (near the annealing point, above the strain point) and is then cooled slowly under control. Un-annealed glass can shatter spontaneously or under minimal impact. Annealing quality is checked with a polariscope (strain viewer).
Surface coatings and treatments
Hot-end coating: tin tetrachloride or titanium tetrachloride vapour applied at about 500 °C, forming a thin SnO2 or TiO2 film that heals surface micro-cracks and anchors the cold-end coating.

Cold-end coating: polyethylene wax or stearate emulsion applied at about 100 °C for lubricity, so bottles do not scratch each other on filling lines (surface scratches cut glass strength by up to 60 percent).

Interior surface treatment (dealkalisation): sulfur dioxide or ammonium sulfate introduced at the hot end converts surface sodium to sodium sulfate, which is washed away, leaving a silica-rich inner skin with improved hydrolytic resistance. This is the "interior coating" concept in the syllabus; it reduces alkali extraction into acidic beverages and pharmaceuticals.
Closures: crown cork (beer, carbonated drinks), lug cap with plastisol liner (vacuum-sealed jars; the safety button indicates loss of vacuum), roll-on pilfer-proof (ROPP) aluminium caps.

Statutory note: FSS (Packaging) Regulations, 2018, Schedule II covers glass containers, requiring conformity to the listed Indian Standards and freedom from defects that could lead to breakage or fragments.
1.3 Metal packaging
1.3.1 Tinplate
Tinplate is low-carbon mild steel (about 0.15 to 0.5 mm) electrolytically coated with tin. From the steel outwards the structure is:
Steel base: strength and formability.
Iron-tin alloy layer (FeSn2): formed during reflow melting of the electrodeposited tin; improves corrosion resistance.
Free tin layer: sacrificial and corrosion resistant.

Passivation film: chromium oxide produced by cathodic treatment in sodium dichromate solution (the common "311" passivation); prevents tin oxide growth and sulfide staining, and improves lacquer adhesion.
Oil film: dioctyl sebacate (DOS) or similar, a few mg/m², for lubrication during handling and forming.

Electrolytic tinplate (ETP) replaced hot-dipped tinplate from the 1930s and allows differential coating (different tin mass on inside and outside). Coating mass ranges from 2.8 to 11.2 g/m² per side (grades such as E2.8/2.8, E5.6/2.8, E11.2/5.6). Heavier tin is used for unlacquered (plain) cans of acidic fruit products.

Why plain tin cans work for some fruits: in de-aerated acidic fruit packs tin is anodic to steel, so tin dissolves slowly and sacrificially, protecting the steel from pitting; the slight tin pickup is harmless below the FSSAI limit of 250 mg/kg and even preserves colour by reducing anthocyanin oxidation. In the presence of residual oxygen, nitrates or certain pigments the polarity can reverse and rapid detinning or hydrogen swell follows.

Can corrosion and spoilage vocabulary: hydrogen swell (internal corrosion liberates hydrogen; "hydrogen springer"), flipper, springer, soft swell, hard swell (the last three progressively indicate gas from microbial spoilage), sulfide black (iron sulfide staining), and pinholing.

HPSC EXAM TRAP: C-enamel
C-enamel is chosen to prevent black sulfide discolouration in sulfur-rich protein foods (corn, peas, meat, fish). It is not chosen for "better corrosion resistance in acid fruits"; that is R-enamel or heavy-tin plain cans. If a question pairs "C-enamel: acid fruits", mark it wrong.

Can construction: three-piece cans (body with welded side seam plus two ends; lead solder is banned) and two-piece cans (drawn and wall-ironed, DWI, for beverages; drawn and redrawn, DRD, for food). The double seam (body hook, cover hook, overlap, sealing compound) is the hermetic closure and is inspected by seam tear-down (overlap, tightness rating). Tin-free steel (electrolytically chromium-coated steel, ECCS) carries chromium and chromium oxide instead of tin; it must be lacquered on both sides, cannot be soldered, and is used for ends and for welded bodies.
1.3.2 Aluminium
Density 2.7 g/cm³ versus 7.8 for steel: lightweight, lower transport energy; alloy 3004 for can bodies, 5182 for easy-open ends.

Spontaneous passive Al2O3 film gives corrosion resistance in neutral media and immunity to sulfide staining; however aluminium is attacked by acids and alkalis and by chloride (pitting), so food cans are always lacquered (epoxy or polyester).
Two-piece DWI beverage cans with stay-on-tab easy-open ends; non-magnetic, so separation at recycling uses eddy-current separators.

Aluminium foil: rolled to 6 to 200 µm; food foil is annealed (soft temper); it has dead-fold (keeps a crease), is opaque (total light barrier), heat-stable, and when pinhole-free offers essentially zero OTR and WVTR.

The foil thickness to pinhole relationship: pinholes arise from rolling inclusions and double rolling of thin gauges. Below about 15 µm (some references say 17 µm) the pinhole count rises steeply; a 9 µm foil may carry several hundred pinholes per square metre, a 7 µm foil even more. Hence:
Foil above 15 µm (for example 20 µm semi-rigid trays, household foil) can be used alone as a near-absolute barrier.

Foil of 6 to 12 µm is always laminated to plastic films (PET on the outside, polyolefin on the inside); the polymer layers bridge pinholes so the laminate behaves as a near-total barrier even though the foil itself is not.
The retort pouch uses 9 to 12 µm foil for exactly this reason.

HPSC EXAM TRAP: foil and "100 percent barrier"
A thin foil is a 100 percent barrier only in the laminate, not on its own. The correct statement is: "aluminium foil below 15 µm is prone to pinholes and is therefore laminated".

blocks.text: 1.4.1 Polyethylene family: LDPE, LLDPE, HDPE
All three are chains of CH2 units; the difference is branching, which controls crystallinity, which controls density, stiffness, melting point and barrier.

LDPE is made at 1000 to 3000 bar by free-radical polymerisation; backbiting creates long branches that prevent close packing. Result: low density, low crystallinity, excellent clarity, flexibility and the best heat-sealability (wide sealing window, seals through light contamination), but poor oxygen, aroma and grease barrier.

LLDPE is made at low pressure with Ziegler-Natta or metallocene catalysts by copolymerising ethylene with an alpha-olefin, so branches are short and uniform. It has similar density to LDPE but higher tensile, puncture and tear strength and a higher melting point, giving down-gauging (thinner films with the same strength) and hot-tack strength for form-fill-seal machines. It is slightly hazier and harder to process than LDPE, so LDPE and LLDPE are commonly blended.

HDPE is linear with almost no branching; chains pack tightly, giving the highest density, stiffness, melting point and the best moisture barrier of the three, but translucency rather than clarity. It is environmentally stress-cracking sensitive with surfactants unless high molecular weight grades are used.

HPSC EXAM TRAP: density ordering
Correct ascending order of density: PP (0.90) < LDPE and LLDPE (0.91 to 0.925) < HDPE (0.94 to 0.965) < EVOH (1.12 to 1.20) < PET (1.33 to 1.40) < PVC (1.35 to 1.45) < PVDC (1.6 to 1.7). Polyolefins float in water; PET, PVC and PVDC sink.
1.4.2 Polypropylene: PP, BOPP, CPP

Isotactic PP (all methyl groups on one side, Ziegler-Natta catalysed) crystallises to a stiff, glossy polymer with the lowest density and the highest melting point of the common polyolefins. Consequences:
Retortable and hot-fillable (Tm 160 to 170 °C) whereas PE deforms at 121 °C.
Poor low-temperature impact: homopolymer PP becomes brittle below about 0 °C, so frozen-food and retort grades use ethylene-propylene random or block copolymers.

BOPP (biaxially oriented, tenter frame) gives high clarity, stiffness, twist retention and improved moisture barrier; metallised BOPP is the standard snack-food film; acrylic or PVDC coatings add sealability and barrier.

CPP (cast polypropylene, chill-roll cast, unoriented) is soft, tough, clear and heat-sealable at 150 to 170 °C, and is the inner food-contact sealant layer of retort pouches because it survives 121 to 135 °C sterilisation without delaminating or losing seal strength. Random copolymer CPP (ethylene-modified) is preferred for low-temperature toughness.
1.4.3 Polyethylene terephthalate (PET)

PET is a condensation polyester of purified terephthalic acid (or dimethyl terephthalate) and ethylene glycol, usually polymerised with an antimony trioxide catalyst (hence the antimony specific migration limit of 0.04 mg/kg). Bottles are injection moulded as preforms, reheated to about 100 °C (above Tg) and stretch-blow moulded; biaxial stretching induces strain crystallisation, giving high strength, clarity and the gas barrier that holds 3 to 4 volumes of carbon dioxide in carbonated soft drinks for several months. Heat-set PET tolerates hot filling at 85 to 90 °C; crystallised CPET trays are oven and microwave stable.

Acetaldehyde and why a scavenger is needed: during melt processing at 270 to 290 °C PET undergoes thermal chain scission to vinyl ester end groups, which rearrange to release acetaldehyde (CH3CHO). Acetaldehyde dissolves in the bottle wall and slowly migrates into the contents, giving a fruity, sweetish off-flavour detectable in still water at about 10 to 20 µg/L (it is masked in flavoured colas but obvious in packaged drinking water). Control measures: low-acetaldehyde resin grades, solid-state polycondensation, careful melt temperature and residence time, and acetaldehyde scavengers such as anthranilamide (2-aminobenzamide), added at a few hundred mg/kg, which reacts with acetaldehyde to form a non-volatile quinazolinone. The Bureau of Indian Standards specification for PET bottles for packaged drinking water prescribes acetaldehyde control for this reason.

Barrier enhancement for oxygen-sensitive beverages (beer, juice): multilayer PET/EVOH/PET or PET/MXD6 nylon, plasma coatings of silicon oxide (SiOx) or diamond-like carbon on the inner surface, and oxygen-scavenging resins (cobalt-catalysed MXD6).
1.4.4 PVC and PVDC

PVC: polymer of vinyl chloride monomer (VCM is a confirmed human carcinogen; residual VCM in packaging is restricted to 1 mg/kg and non-detectable migration under EU rules). Unplasticised PVC (uPVC) is rigid and clear and was widely used for mineral water and edible oil bottles in India before PET displaced it; it has good oil and grease resistance, moderate oxygen barrier, and only moderate moisture barrier. Plasticised PVC (30 to 40 percent plasticiser such as DEHP, DOA, DINP) gives cling film with self-adhesion and high oxygen permeability (useful for fresh meat bloom), but plasticiser migration into fatty foods is the chief regulatory concern (Part 3). PVC softens at about 80 °C (not retortable) and liberates hydrogen chloride and dioxins on uncontrolled incineration.

PVDC: polyvinylidene chloride copolymerised with vinyl chloride or methyl acrylate (Saran, Dow, 1933). Its high chlorine content and high crystallinity give an outstanding barrier to oxygen, water vapour and aromas, and unlike EVOH its barrier does not deteriorate with humidity. Because pure PVDC is hard to process (it degrades near its melting point, releasing HCl), it is mostly used as a thin coating (K-coating) on cellophane, BOPP, PET and nylon, as a shrink film for cheese and processed meat, and as chub-pack film. Drawbacks: yellowing on ageing, chlorine content (environmental objection), not suitable for high-temperature retorting as a monolayer.

HPSC EXAM TRAP: PVC is not PVDC
PVC = one chlorine per repeat unit, moderate barrier, plasticiser migration issue. PVDC = two chlorines per repeat unit, excellent dual barrier, used as a coating. A statement "PVC offers excellent oxygen and moisture barrier" is false; the same sentence about PVDC is true.
1.4.5 Ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH)

EVOH is made by hydrolysing ethylene-vinyl acetate copolymer (pure polyvinyl alcohol cannot be melt-processed and is water-soluble, so ethylene is copolymerised in). The dense hydrogen bonding between hydroxyl groups and the high crystallinity give the lowest oxygen permeability of any melt-processable polymer (dry OTR of the order of 0.1 to 1 cm³/m²·day for a 25 µm film, two to three orders of magnitude better than PET). Trade-offs:
Lower ethylene content (27 to 32 mol percent): best gas barrier, worst moisture sensitivity, harder to process.
Higher ethylene content (44 to 48 mol percent): better processability and humidity tolerance, poorer barrier.

At relative humidity above about 75 percent, water plasticises the hydroxyl network and OTR rises ten to a hundred fold; after retorting the laminate suffers "retort shock" (temporary barrier loss) that recovers as the layer dries.

Therefore EVOH is never used alone: it is co-extruded as a thin core between polyolefin skins with maleic-anhydride-grafted tie layers (for example PP/tie/EVOH/tie/PP), where the hydrophobic skins keep the core dry. Applications: squeezable ketchup and mayonnaise bottles, retortable transparent trays and pouches (foil replacement for microwaveable products), cheese and processed meat films, modified atmosphere trays.
1.5 Retort pouches
Definition and origin

A retort pouch is a flexible, heat-sealable, hermetically sealed laminate container capable of withstanding thermal sterilisation at 115 to 135 °C (commonly 121 °C for 20 to 40 minutes, delivering commercial sterility expressed as an F0 value) so that low-acid foods are shelf stable at ambient temperature without refrigeration. It was developed in the 1960s and 1970s by the United States Army Natick Laboratories with Reynolds Metals and Continental Flexible Packaging for military rations (Meal, Ready-to-Eat) and is now used for curries, ready meals, tuna, pet food and rice.

blocks.text: The three-ply pouch is PET / Al / CPP; the four-ply pouch is PET / Al / OPA / CPP (nylon placed between the foil and the sealant). Layers are bonded by adhesive lamination with two-component polyurethane adhesives, which must be fully cured before filling to avoid primary aromatic amine migration (Part 3). Transparent and microwaveable retort pouches replace foil with PET/SiOx, PET/AlOx or EVOH-based barrier layers at some sacrifice of shelf life.
Heat penetration dynamics versus the cylindrical tinplate can

Thermal sterilisation of a conduction-heating food is unsteady-state conduction, and the time for the slowest-heating point (cold spot) to reach a target temperature scales with the square of the characteristic conduction distance. A 307 × 409 can (73 mm diameter, 115 mm height) has a cold-spot conduction path of about 36 mm; a filled retort pouch is a thin slab 15 to 25 mm thick, with a half-thickness of only 8 to 12 mm. Consequences:
Process time at the same retort temperature is cut by 30 to 50 percent for the same F0, because the whole pouch heats almost uniformly.
Less overcooking of the surface layers while waiting for the centre: better retention of thiamine, vitamin C, colour, texture and flavour; the product tastes closer to freshly cooked.
Lower energy per unit, faster cooling, lower steam and water consumption.

Requirements that cans do not impose: the pouch must be processed in an overpressure retort (steam-air or water immersion or spray) because internal vapour pressure at 121 °C would otherwise burst the seals; pouches are held flat in racks to control thickness; residual air must be minimised (under about 10 mL, by vacuum or steam-flush sealing) since trapped air insulates, floats the pouch and promotes oxidation; seal areas must be clean, and seals are tested for strength, burst pressure and leakage.

After processing, pouches require a carton for distribution (less rigid than cans) and quality control includes an incubation test (typically 37 °C for 10 days, with 55 °C incubation for thermophilic checks) as prescribed in FSSAI's commercial sterility requirements for canned and retorted foods.

2.0 Definitions that examiners quote

Active packaging: packaging in which the package, the product and the environment interact deliberately to extend shelf life, improve safety or sensory quality, while maintaining quality; the EU definition (Regulation (EC) 1935/2004 and Regulation (EC) 450/2009) is that active materials "deliberately incorporate components that would release or absorb substances into or from the packaged food or the environment surrounding the food". Active packaging acts.

Intelligent (smart) packaging: materials and articles that monitor the condition of packaged food or the environment surrounding the food and communicate that information. Intelligent packaging informs; it does not change the food.

Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP): replacement of the air in the package with a defined gas mixture at the time of packing, after which the atmosphere is not controlled (distinguish from controlled atmosphere storage, where gas composition is actively maintained in a store).

blocks.text: 2.1 Oxygen scavengers

Oxygen drives lipid oxidation (rancidity, loss of essential fatty acids and vitamins A, C, E), oxidative browning and pigment loss, and growth of aerobic spoilage organisms including moulds. Vacuum and gas flushing leave 0.5 to 2 percent residual oxygen; a scavenger drives headspace oxygen below 0.01 percent (100 ppm) and keeps absorbing oxygen that permeates through the film during storage.
Iron-based sachets (Ageless by Mitsubishi Gas Chemical, 1977; FreshPax, Oxy-Guard)
Finely divided reduced iron powder with an electrolyte (sodium chloride) and a moisture donor, packed in an oxygen-permeable but food-grade sachet. The reaction is electrochemical rusting:
4Fe + 3O2 + 6H2O → 4Fe(OH)3

Stoichiometry: 4 moles of iron (about 223 g) consume 3 moles of oxygen (about 67 L at standard conditions), so 1 g of iron absorbs roughly 300 mL of oxygen; sachets are graded by capacity (for example 100 or 200 mL oxygen). Moisture-dependent types need a food water activity above about 0.65; self-reacting types carry their own moisture and work in dry foods. Advantages: cheap, high capacity, rapid. Disadvantages: sachet can be accidentally ingested (must be labelled "do not eat"; not permitted loose in some infant foods), iron is detected by in-line metal detectors so sachet insertion must be sequenced after detection or non-ferrous scavengers used, sachets are unsuitable for liquids and for microwave heating, and the pack can collapse as oxygen is removed (compensated by combining with a carbon dioxide emitter).

2.3 Ethylene absorbers

Ethylene (C2H4) is the gaseous ripening hormone; concentrations as low as 0.1 ppm trigger the climacteric rise in respiration of bananas, mangoes, apples, tomatoes and avocados, accelerate chlorophyll loss in leafy vegetables and cause russet spotting of lettuce. Removing it from the package or store extends shelf life.

Potassium permanganate system: KMnO4 (4 to 6 percent) impregnated on a porous inert carrier (alumina, silica gel, zeolite, vermiculite, perlite) oxidises ethylene stepwise to acetaldehyde, then acetic acid, then carbon dioxide and water; the overall reaction can be written 3C2H4 + 12KMnO4 → 12MnO2 + 12KOH + 6CO2 + 6H2O. The colour change from purple (permanganate) to brown (manganese dioxide) indicates exhaustion. Because permanganate is toxic and strongly oxidising it is never incorporated in food-contact film; it is used only in sachets, blankets or filters in cartons and cold stores. Other absorbers: activated carbon with palladium catalyst, zeolite- or clay-loaded polyethylene films (sold in Japan and Korea, limited capacity), and ethylene-oxidising catalysts in ripening rooms. Note that 1-methylcyclopropene (SmartFresh) is a ripening inhibitor applied as a gas treatment, not a packaging absorber.
2.4 Antimicrobial packaging

Antimicrobial agents are either released from the package to the food surface (migrating systems, suitable where surface contamination governs spoilage, such as sliced meat and cheese) or immobilised on the film surface (non-migrating, contact-active systems).

blocks.text: 2.5 Carbon dioxide emitters and absorbers

Carbon dioxide at 20 to 100 percent is bacteriostatic and fungistatic (it dissolves in the aqueous phase, lowers pH and interferes with enzymes of Pseudomonas, Enterobacteriaceae and moulds), but it dissolves into the food, which causes pack collapse in modified atmosphere packs. A CO2 emitter compensates:
Sodium bicarbonate with citric or ascorbic acid, activated by product moisture: NaHCO3 + H+ → Na+ + CO2 + H2O. Used in pads under fresh meat, poultry and fish.

Dual-function sachets (iron oxygen scavenger with ferrous carbonate or ascorbate plus bicarbonate, for example Ageless G) absorb oxygen and emit an equal volume of carbon dioxide to keep the pack full.

Carbon dioxide absorbers: freshly roasted coffee releases carbon dioxide for days and would burst a hermetic pack; calcium hydroxide sachets absorb it, Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O; the alternative is a one-way degassing valve in the pack. Absorbers are also used for kimchi and other fermenting foods.
2.6 Modified atmosphere packaging and vacuum packaging

Gases used: oxygen (maintains the cherry-red oxymyoglobin of fresh meat, allows respiration of produce, prevents anaerobic growth), carbon dioxide (antimicrobial, soluble), nitrogen (inert filler preventing collapse, displaces oxygen in snacks), and in some countries carbon monoxide (colour fixation of meat; not permitted in India and the EU) and argon.

blocks.text: Safety points for the Food Safety Officer: MAP does not sterilise; it only slows spoilage at chill temperature, and by suppressing spoilage organisms it may let pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes and non-proteolytic Clostridium botulinum reach hazardous levels without obvious spoilage, so strict temperature control (below 3.3 °C for vacuum-packed fish) and shelf-life validation are essential. Vacuum packaging removes air without replacing it and depends on an oxygen-barrier film (PA/PE, PVDC-coated) and refrigeration.
2.7 Intelligent packaging systems
2.7.1 Time-temperature indicators (TTIs)

A TTI is a device whose irreversible, visible response integrates the temperature history (full-history TTI) or signals only that a threshold was crossed (critical temperature indicator, partial history). The reaction rate follows Arrhenius kinetics; a TTI is matched to a food when its activation energy is within about 25 kJ/mol of the activation energy of the food's deterioration (for example microbial growth in chilled fish, about 60 to 90 kJ/mol).

2.7.2 Freshness and spoilage indicators
These respond to metabolites of spoilage rather than to temperature history.

Volatile amines: spoilage of fish and meat releases trimethylamine (from trimethylamine oxide by Shewanella and Photobacterium), dimethylamine, ammonia and biogenic amines, collectively measured as total volatile basic nitrogen (TVB-N). Amines are alkaline and raise headspace pH; indicator films containing bromocresol green, bromophenol blue, bromothymol blue, methyl red, chlorophenol red or natural anthocyanins change colour (COX Technologies FreshTag for fish; many anthocyanin-based research films).
Hydrogen sulfide: poultry spoilage indicators using myoglobin-based pigments that convert to sulfmyoglobin (green).
Carbon dioxide: bromothymol-blue or methyl-red based indicators for kimchi and MAP integrity.
Aroma: RipeSense (New Zealand) senses aromatic volatiles from ripening pears and changes from red to orange to yellow.
Pathogen or toxin biosensors: antibody-based labels (for example FoodSentinel barcode that becomes unreadable when a target pathogen binds) remain largely developmental.
2.7.3 Integrity (leak) indicators: oxygen indicators based on redox dyes

The classic oxygen indicator tablet (Ageless Eye, Mitsubishi) contains methylene blue, a reducing sugar (glucose) and an alkali in a gel. In an oxygen-free pack (below about 0.1 percent oxygen) the dye is in its reduced leuco form and appears pink; when oxygen enters through a pinhole or a failed seal (above about 0.5 percent) methylene blue is re-oxidised and turns blue, usually within minutes. It is used inside packs with oxygen scavengers and in modified atmosphere packs to show seal failure, and it reverts if oxygen is scavenged again, which is a limitation for tamper evidence. Related systems use ultraviolet-activated titanium dioxide and methylene blue in printed inks for irreversible indication.
2.7.4 Data carriers: barcodes and RFID

Barcodes: linear EAN-13 (the 13-digit code on retail packs, administered in India by GS1 India, prefix 890) carry only an identifier; two-dimensional GS1 DataMatrix and QR codes carry batch, expiry and serial numbers and support consumer access to FSSAI licence details and recall information.

RFID (radio-frequency identification): a tag (microchip plus antenna) is read without line of sight; passive tags are powered by the reader field, active tags carry a battery. Frequencies: low frequency about 125 kHz (short range, animal identification), high frequency 13.56 MHz (near-field communication, smart phones, library and item level), ultra-high frequency 860 to 960 MHz (pallet and case level, several metres read range). Benefits: automatic traceability (one step back, one step forward as required by FSSAI licensing conditions and Codex), cold-chain data when combined with temperature sensors, rapid recall, anti-counterfeiting. Limitations: cost per tag, interference from metals and liquids, data privacy.

HPSC EXAM TRAP: active versus intelligent
A time-temperature indicator, a freshness indicator and an oxygen leak indicator are intelligent packaging (they inform). An oxygen scavenger, an ethylene absorber and an antimicrobial film are active packaging (they act). Statements that classify a scavenger as intelligent, or an indicator as active, are wrong. Also, a TTI tracks temperature history, not the actual microbial state of the food; a freshness indicator tracks spoilage metabolites, not temperature.
Part 3. Migration Chemistry & FSSAI Packaging Regulations 2018
PART 3: MIGRATION CHEMISTRY AND FSS (PACKAGING) REGULATIONS, 2018
3.1 Migration from first principles

Migration is the mass transfer of substances from a food contact material into the food (or a simulant) by diffusion. The migrating substances are starting substances (monomers, catalysts such as antimony), additives (plasticisers, antioxidants, slip agents, colourants), processing aids, adhesive and ink components, and non-intentionally added substances (NIAS) such as oligomers, degradation products and impurities.

Kinetics: migration obeys Fick's second law; early migration grows with the square root of contact time and later approaches equilibrium set by the partition coefficient between polymer and food. Migration increases with temperature (retorting, microwaving, hot filling), contact time, fat content of the food (lipophilic migrants partition into oil), decreasing molecular weight of the migrant (substances above about 1000 Da are considered not to be absorbed from the gut and are exempt from toxicological evaluation), and polymer mobility (polyolefins have high diffusivity, PET and polystyrene low). Migration also occurs through the gas phase (volatile ink components and mineral oil from paperboard) and by set-off (printed outer surface transferring ink to the food-contact side in a reel or stack).

Functional barrier concept: a layer (for example aluminium foil or thick PET) that reduces migration from layers behind it to below the detection limit allows the use of non-approved substances behind it, subject to a no-carcinogen rule.

Passing the overall migration test does not prove safety; a material can be below 60 mg/kg overall and still exceed the SML of a potent migrant such as BPA or a primary aromatic amine. Conversely a high overall migration (for example from a plasticised PVC) can occur with every individual SML met. Both tests are required.

blocks.text: 3.5 Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations, 2018
Legislative lineage

Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006: Section 3(1)(zz) defines unsafe food and includes food rendered injurious by the packaging in which it is contained; Section 16 empowers the Food Authority to specify standards for packaging; packaging that renders food unsafe attracts penalties under Section 59 (unsafe food) and related sections.
FSS (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011: combined packaging and labelling provisions.

FSS (Packaging) Regulations, 2018: notified in the Gazette on 24 December 2018 and enforced from 1 July 2019, carving packaging out as a stand-alone regulation; the labelling provisions were later replaced by the FSS (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020.

Interlocking rules: Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 (Ministry of Environment), which prohibit the use of recycled plastics and carry bags made of recycled plastic for storing, carrying, dispensing or packaging ready-to-eat or ready-to-drink food, set carry-bag thickness (raised to 75 µm from 30 September 2021 and 120 µm from 31 December 2022) and banned identified single-use plastic items (plastic cutlery, straws, stirrers, earbuds, wrapping films around sweet boxes) from 1 July 2022; and Bureau of Indian Standards specifications referenced in the Schedules.
Structure of the 2018 Regulations

Material-wise requirements for paper and board, glass, metal and metal alloys, and plastics, cross-referring to the Schedules; for plastics: conformity to listed IS specifications, overall migration not exceeding 60 mg/kg or 10 mg/dm² when tested per IS 9845, specific migration limits for listed metals and DEHP, and the prohibition on recycled plastics and on products made of recycled plastics for packaging, storing, carrying or dispensing food

The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive 94/62/EC sets a benchmark of 100 mg/kg for the sum of lead, cadmium, mercury and hexavalent chromium in packaging material; migration of lead from plastics under the EU specific limits is at the 0.01 to 1 mg/kg level depending on the article class. Candidates should quote the Gazette text of Schedule IV in the descriptive paper and avoid inventing figures.
Absolute prohibitions and their scientific basis

Newspaper and similar printed materials shall not be used for wrapping, packing or serving food (FSSAI advisory of 2016 incorporated in Regulation 3). Basis: newspaper inks contain mineral oil hydrocarbons, solvents, pigments with lead and other metals and sometimes chemical driers; the paper is handled unhygienically and carries microbial load; lipophilic ink components migrate readily into fried and oily street foods. The common sight of pakoras drained on newspaper is therefore a punishable violation.

Recycled plastics and products made of recycled plastics (including carry bags) shall not be used for packaging, storing, carrying or dispensing food. Basis: unknown prior use, contamination with non-food chemicals, degradation products and unapproved additives. Exception: FSSAI's subsequent amendment framework and Bureau of Indian Standards IS 17899 T (2022) allow recycled PET and other recycled plastics for food contact only when produced by an FSSAI-approved or certified food-grade recycling process with decontamination challenge testing, in line with Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules; recycled material used behind a functional barrier is treated separately. In an examination answer: "prohibited, except certified food-grade recycled plastic produced under FSSAI-recognised processes".

Printed surface of packaging shall not come in direct contact with food, so printed recycled paper, printed carry bags and reverse-printed films where the print faces inward are not acceptable; printing inks must conform to IS 15495.
Packaging must not impart undesirable odour, colour or taste, and must not transfer substances harmful to health; this is the general safety clause under which any novel migrant can be acted upon.
Plastics in contact with food must be made only of listed polymers conforming to listed Indian Standards; carbon black and pigments only per IS 9833.
Tin coating and lacquers for metal containers must conform to the listed standards; lead-soldered cans are not permitted.

HPSC EXAM TRAP: absolute-qualifier phrasing on prohibitions
"Newspaper may be used for wrapping dry foods if clean": false, the prohibition is absolute. "Recycled plastics are permitted for food contact": false as a general statement, but "recycled plastics are permitted only when certified food-grade under FSSAI-recognised processes" is true. "The overall migration limit applies to glass": false, it applies to plastics (glass is treated as inert and controlled by specification). "The 2018 Packaging Regulations also cover labelling": false, labelling is in the 2020 Labelling and Display Regulations.
Migration testing workflow a Food Safety Officer should be able to describe
Identify the packaging material, layer structure and intended use (food type, contact time, temperature).
Select simulants from the food classification (aqueous, acidic, alcoholic, fatty, dry) and the time-temperature condition matching the worst foreseeable use.
Expose a known surface area (for example 1 dm²) to a known volume of simulant (for example 100 mL, giving 6 dm² per kg convention) by total immersion, pouch filling or cell method.

Overall migration: evaporate the aqueous simulant to dryness, weigh the residue, correct for blank, express as mg/dm² and convert to mg/kg; for oil, determine the weight loss of the specimen corrected for oil uptake.
Specific migration: analyse the simulant by HPLC-UV or LC-MS/MS (phthalates, BPA, PAAs, benzophenone), GC-MS (volatiles, styrene, vinyl chloride), ICP-MS or AAS (metals).
Compare against the OML and SMLs, issue the NABL certificate of conformity, and in enforcement draw samples under Section 38 of the Act for referral to the Food Analyst.
Part 4A. Instrumental Food Analysis
PART 4A: INSTRUMENTAL FOOD ANALYSIS
4.0 Chromatography from first principles
Chromatography separates components of a mixture by their differential partitioning between a stationary phase and a mobile phase that moves past it. Key quantities:
Retention factor k = (tR − t0)/t0, where tR is the retention time of the analyte and t0 the hold-up time of an unretained compound.
Selectivity α = k2/k1 for two adjacent peaks.
Column efficiency as number of theoretical plates N = 16 (tR/W)², where W is the baseline peak width; plate height H = L/N.
Resolution Rs = 2 (tR2 − tR1)/(W1 + W2); Rs of 1.5 is baseline separation.

Van Deemter equation H = A + B/u + C·u: A is eddy diffusion (multiple flow paths through packed particles), B/u is longitudinal diffusion (dominant at low linear velocity u), C·u is resistance to mass transfer (dominant at high velocity). Open-tubular capillary GC columns have no A term (Golay equation), which is why they are far more efficient than packed columns; in HPLC, smaller particles (sub-2 µm in UHPLC) shrink A and C, raising efficiency at the price of back-pressure above 600 bar.

The practical rule for choosing a technique: volatile and thermally stable analytes (fatty acid esters, pesticides, flavour volatiles, solvents) go to GC; non-volatile, polar or thermolabile analytes (vitamins, colours, mycotoxins, sugars, antibiotics, carbamate pesticides, acrylamide) go to HPLC or LC-MS/MS; elements go to AAS or ICP-MS.
4.1 High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)
Instrumentation

Solvent reservoirs and degasser: HPLC-grade solvents (water, acetonitrile, methanol, buffers), filtered through 0.45 or 0.22 µm membranes and degassed (helium sparging or vacuum degasser) to prevent bubbles in the pump and detector.

Pump: dual-piston reciprocating pump delivering 0.1 to 10 mL/min against 100 to 400 bar (up to 1200 bar in UHPLC) with pulse dampening; isocratic elution (constant composition) or gradient elution (composition changed with time to elute strongly retained compounds faster) using low-pressure (proportioning valve before one pump) or high-pressure (two pumps) mixing.
Injector: six-port rotary valve (Rheodyne) with a fixed loop of 5 to 100 µL, loaded at atmospheric pressure and switched into the high-pressure stream; autosamplers automate this.

Column: stainless steel tube, typically 150 to 250 mm long and 4.6 mm internal diameter, packed with 3 to 5 µm porous silica particles chemically bonded with the stationary phase. Reversed-phase columns carry octadecylsilane (ODS, C18) non-polar chains and are used with polar aqueous mobile phases; less polar analytes are retained longer. Normal-phase (bare silica, amino, cyano) retains polar compounds; ion-exchange, size-exclusion, HILIC and chiral phases serve special needs. A guard column protects the analytical column; a column oven (25 to 60 °C) stabilises retention.
Detector (see table), data system for integration and quantitation by external standard, internal standard or standard addition.

HPSC EXAM TRAP: RID and gradients
The refractive index detector cannot be used with gradient elution because any change in mobile phase composition changes the refractive index and the baseline; it also needs tight temperature control and has the poorest sensitivity. A statement "RID is the detector of choice for trace analysis with gradient HPLC" is wrong on two counts.
Applications

Vitamins: fat-soluble vitamins (A as retinol, D2 and D3, E as tocopherols, K1) are released by alkaline saponification (ethanolic KOH with pyrogallol or BHT antioxidant), extracted into hexane or diethyl ether and determined by reversed-phase HPLC with UV or fluorescence detection; water-soluble B vitamins (B1, B2, B3, B6, folate, B12) are extracted by acid and enzymatic (takadiastase, phosphatase) hydrolysis and separated by ion-pair reversed-phase HPLC with UV, fluorescence (B1 after oxidation to thiochrome, B2 native) or MS detection; vitamin C is extracted in metaphosphoric acid and measured at about 245 nm, with dithiothreitol reduction to include dehydroascorbic acid. Relevant for verifying nutrition labels under the Labelling and Display Regulations and fortification claims under the Fortification Regulations.

Synthetic food colours: India permits eight synthetic colours (Ponceau 4R, Carmoisine, Erythrosine, Tartrazine, Sunset Yellow FCF, Indigo Carmine, Brilliant Blue FCF and Fast Green FCF) with a general ceiling of 100 mg/kg (200 mg/kg in specified products such as certain canned fruits and sweets) singly or in combination, only in listed foods. Non-permitted colours (Metanil Yellow, Rhodamine B, Orange II, Sudan dyes, Auramine, Malachite Green) are frequent adulterants of sweets, spices and beverages. Colours are extracted by adsorption on wool or polyamide, or by solid-phase extraction, and separated by reversed-phase ion-pair HPLC with PDA detection; each colour is identified by retention time plus its visible spectrum, allowing a single run to screen permitted and non-permitted dyes. Screening methods: thin-layer chromatography and spot tests under the FSSAI manual.

Aflatoxins: aflatoxins B1, B2, G1 and G2 (Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus in groundnuts, maize, chillies, nuts, copra) and M1 (hydroxylated metabolite of B1 secreted in milk) are extracted with methanol-water or acetonitrile-water, cleaned up on immunoaffinity columns bearing anti-aflatoxin antibodies, eluted with methanol and separated on a C18 column with water-methanol-acetonitrile. B2 and G2 fluoresce strongly in aqueous mobile phase, but B1 and G1 (with a terminal double bond in the dihydrofuran ring) show quenched fluorescence; so post-column derivatisation is applied: reaction with iodine in a heated reactor, electrochemically generated bromine (Kobra cell), or a photochemical reactor (ultraviolet irradiation forming hydrated derivatives), each of which saturates the double bond and restores fluorescence; pre-column trifluoroacetic acid derivatisation is the alternative. Detection: Ex 365 nm, Em 435 to 450 nm. FSSAI limits (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations as amended): total aflatoxins 15 µg/kg and aflatoxin B1 10 µg/kg in cereals, nuts and oilseeds; aflatoxin M1 0.5 µg/kg in milk. 4.2 Gas chromatography (GC and GC-MS)
4.2.1 First principles

Gas chromatography separates volatile and thermally stable analytes (boiling point generally below about 400 °C, molecular mass below about 600 Da) by partitioning them between an inert gaseous mobile phase, which merely carries the analyte and does not interact with it, and a liquid stationary phase coated on the inner wall of a capillary column. Retention is governed by the vapour pressure of the analyte at the column temperature (hence boiling-point order on non-polar columns) and by the polarity match between analyte and stationary phase. Because retention depends exponentially on temperature, temperature programming (for example 60 °C held 2 minutes, then 10 °C per minute to 300 °C) is used to elute both light and heavy components with good peak shape in one run. Non-volatile analytes (fatty acids, sugars, amino acids, sterols) are first converted to volatile derivatives (methylation, silylation, acylation).

HPSC EXAM TRAP: FID versus ECD
FID is the universal carbon detector with the widest linear range and is destructive. ECD is the selective halogen detector, uses a 63Ni beta source, is the most sensitive for organochlorine pesticides, is non-destructive, and has the narrowest linear range. A statement that ECD responds to all organic compounds, or that FID is used for organochlorine residue screening at µg/kg, is wrong.
4.2.6 GC-MS fundamentals
Interface: the capillary column runs directly into the ion source held under vacuum (10^-5 to 10^-6 torr) maintained by a turbomolecular pump; helium is pumped away.

Electron ionisation (EI): a heated tungsten or rhenium filament emits electrons accelerated through 70 V; collision ejects an electron from the analyte, M + e- → M+• + 2e-, producing the molecular ion, which fragments into characteristic ions. 70 eV is used because ionisation efficiency reaches a plateau there, so small fluctuations do not alter the spectrum and spectra are reproducible between instruments and comparable with libraries (NIST, Wiley, with more than 300000 spectra). Fragmentation follows predictable rules (alpha-cleavage, McLafferty rearrangement, tropylium ion at m/z 91 for benzyl compounds).
Chemical ionisation (CI) with methane, isobutane or ammonia reagent gas is a soft technique giving the protonated molecule [M+H]+ when the molecular ion is absent under EI.
Analysers: single quadrupole (most common), ion trap, time-of-flight (high resolution, exact mass), triple quadrupole GC-MS/MS for pesticide residues with MRM as described for LC-MS/MS.

Acquisition modes: full scan (for identification, library search of unknowns) and selected ion monitoring (SIM, where the quadrupole dwells on two to four characteristic ions per analyte, raising sensitivity 10 to 100 fold; one quantifier ion and qualifier ions whose ratios must match the standard within the tolerances of the EU SANTE pesticide guidance, usually within 30 percent relative).
4.2.7 Derivatisation: fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs)

Triglycerides are non-volatile and free fatty acids tail badly on GC columns because of hydrogen bonding, so lipids are converted to volatile fatty acid methyl esters by transesterification. Two official routes:

Boron trifluoride-methanol (AOAC 969.33, IS 548 Part 3, AOCS Ce 2-66): the fat is first saponified by refluxing with 0.5 N methanolic sodium hydroxide (triglyceride + 3NaOH → glycerol + 3RCOONa), then 12 to 14 percent BF3 in methanol is added and the mixture refluxed at 100 °C for 2 to 5 minutes; the Lewis acid catalyses esterification, RCOOH + CH3OH → RCOOCH3 + H2O, giving quantitative methylation of all acids including free acids and phospholipid acids. Esters are extracted into heptane or hexane after adding saturated sodium chloride solution.

Methanolic potassium hydroxide (ISO 12966-2, IUPAC 2.301, rapid cold method): 2 N KOH in methanol is shaken with the oil dissolved in heptane at room temperature for 1 to 2 minutes; base-catalysed transesterification, RCOOR' + CH3OH → RCOOCH3 + R'OH, proceeds via the methoxide ion. It is fast and avoids heating (no isomerisation of conjugated or polyunsaturated acids) but does not methylate free fatty acids and fails for oils with high acidity.
Alternatives: 2 percent sulfuric acid in methanol (acid catalysed, slow), sodium methoxide, trimethylsulfonium hydroxide (one-step in the injector).

Analysis: 100 m biscyanopropyl polysiloxane column, FID, hydrogen or helium carrier, oven 140 to 240 °C programme, split injection, internal standard C17:0 or C23:0 methyl ester, identification by comparison with a 37-component FAME mix; results expressed as percent of total fatty acids. On the polar column, elution within each carbon number is saturated, then trans, then cis isomers, so elaidic acid (C18:1 trans-9) elutes before oleic acid (C18:1 cis-9), and the sum of the trans peaks gives total trans fatty acids.

Regulatory linkage: FSSAI limits industrially produced trans fatty acids to 2 percent by weight of total fats in all fats and oils and in foods containing fats and oils (effective 1 January 2022, down from 5 percent in 2021 and 10 percent earlier); a trans fat free claim requires not more than 0.2 g per 100 g or 100 mL. The same FAME profile detects adulteration (for example argemone-free but cheaper palm olein in groundnut oil, lard in ghee by Reichert-Meissl and butyric acid C4:0 content, which only milk fat contains at about 3 to 4 percent) and verifies omega-3 claims.
4.2.8 Pesticide residue screening by GC

Sample preparation uses the QuEChERS method (quick, easy, cheap, effective, rugged, safe; AOAC 2007.01, EN 15662): 10 g homogenised produce is shaken with 10 mL acetonitrile, salted out with anhydrous magnesium sulfate and sodium chloride (or citrate buffers), and the extract is cleaned by dispersive solid-phase extraction with primary secondary amine (PSA) sorbent, which removes fatty acids and sugars, plus C18 for fat and graphitised carbon black for chlorophyll. Organochlorines are screened by GC-ECD, organophosphates by GC-NPD or FPD, and all are confirmed by GC-MS or GC-MS/MS. The FSSAI default maximum residue limit for any pesticide not specifically listed in the Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations is 0.01 mg/kg, and DDT, endosulfan, lindane and many organochlorines are banned or restricted under the Insecticides Act, 1968, so their presence at any level is an enforcement issue.
4.3 Tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)
4.3.1 Why LC-MS/MS exists

Most veterinary drugs, mycotoxins, modern pesticides, acrylamide and melamine are polar, thermally labile or non-volatile, so they are unsuited to GC without derivatisation, and in complex food matrices a UV detector cannot distinguish a residue at 1 µg/kg from co-eluting matrix. Coupling HPLC to a triple quadrupole mass spectrometer solves both problems: the liquid chromatograph handles polar molecules, and two stages of mass filtering give selectivity so high that clean-up can be minimal while sensitivity reaches sub-µg/kg.
4.3.2 Atmospheric pressure ionisation: ESI versus APCI
The challenge is to convert ions in a liquid flowing at 0.2 to 1 mL per minute into gas-phase ions at atmospheric pressure, then sample them into the vacuum.

Electrospray ionisation (ESI, John Fenn, Nobel Prize 2002): the eluent passes through a stainless steel capillary held at 3 to 5 kV relative to the counter electrode; the field charges the liquid surface, draws it into a Taylor cone and sprays a fine mist of highly charged droplets, assisted by a coaxial nitrogen nebulising gas. Heated drying gas evaporates solvent, droplets shrink until charge repulsion exceeds surface tension (the Rayleigh limit) and they undergo repeated Coulomb fission; finally ions leave the droplets (ion evaporation model for small molecules; charged residue model for proteins). Ionisation happens in solution, so ESI favours compounds that are already ionic or readily protonated or deprotonated: acids, bases, zwitterions, polar drugs, peptides, proteins (which acquire multiple charges). Positive mode gives [M+H]+ (or [M+Na]+, [M+NH4]+), negative mode gives [M-H]-. ESI is the softest ionisation (no fragmentation, intact molecular information) but is prone to matrix effects: co-eluting matrix components compete for charge and suppress (or enhance) the analyte signal, which is why isotope-labelled internal standards (13C or deuterium) and matrix-matched calibration are mandatory in residue methods.

Atmospheric pressure chemical ionisation (APCI): the eluent is nebulised and vaporised in a heated tube at 350 to 500 °C; a corona discharge needle (about 3 kV) ionises solvent and nitrogen to form reagent ions (H3O+, CH3OH2+), which transfer a proton to the analyte in the gas phase (M + H3O+ → [M+H]+ + H2O). Because ionisation occurs in the gas phase, APCI suits neutral, moderately polar to non-polar, thermally stable molecules of low to medium mass (below about 1500 Da) and gives only singly charged ions; it tolerates higher flow rates and non-polar mobile phases and is less affected by matrix suppression, but cannot be used for thermolabile or very polar or large molecules. Atmospheric pressure photoionisation (APPI, krypton lamp 10 eV) extends the range to non-polar compounds such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and vitamins D and K.

blocks.text: 4.3.3 Triple quadrupole (QqQ) architecture

A quadrupole is four parallel metal rods to which a direct current voltage and a radio-frequency voltage are applied; for a given voltage ratio only ions of one mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) have stable trajectories and pass through, while others strike the rods (described by the Mathieu equations). Scanning the voltages sweeps the transmitted mass. The triple quadrupole arranges three such devices in line:

Q1 (first mass filter): set to transmit only the precursor ion of the target analyte, for example [M+H]+ at m/z 445 for tetracycline. Everything else from the ion source, including matrix ions of other masses, is rejected here.

q2 (collision cell): a radio-frequency-only quadrupole or hexapole (no mass filtering; lower-case q) filled with argon or nitrogen at about 1 to 5 millitorr. The precursor ion is accelerated into the gas (collision energy 5 to 50 eV) and undergoes collision-induced dissociation (CID): kinetic energy is converted to internal energy and the ion breaks at its weakest bonds into product ions and neutral fragments.

Q3 (second mass filter): set to transmit only a specific product ion, for example m/z 410 (loss of ammonia and water from tetracycline). Only an ion that had the correct precursor mass and also produced the correct fragment reaches the detector (electron multiplier), so chemical noise is almost eliminated.

Scan modes derived from this architecture: product ion scan (Q1 fixed, Q3 scanned; used for method development and structure elucidation), precursor ion scan (Q3 fixed, Q1 scanned; finds all compounds giving a common fragment, for example all glucuronides), neutral loss scan (both scanned with a fixed offset), and multiple reaction monitoring.

HPSC EXAM TRAP: q2 is not a mass analyser
In a triple quadrupole the precursor is selected in Q1, fragmented in the collision cell q2 (which only transmits ions and does no mass selection), and the product is selected in Q3. A statement that the collision cell selects the precursor or product ion is wrong.
4.3.4 Multiple reaction monitoring (MRM, also called selected reaction monitoring)

In MRM both Q1 and Q3 are fixed on a precursor-product pair called a transition, with a dwell time of 5 to 100 milliseconds, then switched to the next transition; a modern instrument monitors several hundred transitions in one run using retention-time windows (scheduled MRM). For each analyte at least two transitions are acquired: the most intense (quantifier) for calibration and a second (qualifier) whose ratio to the first must match the reference standard within tolerance (EU Decision 2002/657/EC and SANTE guidance). Identification points: a precursor ion earns 1.0 point and each product ion 1.5 points, so one precursor with two products gives 4 points, which is the minimum required for confirming banned (Group A) substances such as chloramphenicol and nitrofurans; permitted drugs (Group B) need 3 points. Advantages of MRM: selectivity (two-stage filtering), sensitivity (the detector sees only the target ion, giving sub-µg/kg limits), speed (no derivatisation), and the ability to quantify hundreds of residues simultaneously.

blocks.text: 4.4 Atomic spectroscopy for heavy metals
4.4.1 First principles

Atomic absorption relies on free, gaseous, ground-state atoms absorbing light at a resonance wavelength characteristic of the element (lead 283.3 nm, cadmium 228.8 nm, arsenic 193.7 nm, mercury 253.7 nm, copper 324.8 nm, zinc 213.9 nm). According to the Boltzmann distribution, at flame temperatures (2000 to 3000 K) more than 99.9 percent of atoms of most elements are in the ground state, so absorption is far more sensitive and matrix independent than flame emission for all but the easily excited alkali metals (sodium, potassium, lithium, measured by flame photometry). The instrument comprises a hollow cathode lamp of the same element as the analyte (emitting a very narrow line, which is why one lamp per element is needed and AAS is sequential), an atomiser (flame, furnace, quartz cell), a monochromator to isolate the resonance line, a photomultiplier detector, and a background corrector (deuterium continuum lamp or Zeeman effect using a strong magnetic field to split the absorption line). Absorbance follows the Beer-Lambert law, A = ε·b·c, and quantitation uses external calibration, standard addition for difficult matrices, and certified reference materials for validation.

Sample preparation is common to all techniques and is the usual source of error. Wet digestion with concentrated nitric acid and hydrogen peroxide in closed-vessel microwave digesters (180 to 200 °C) is the method of choice because it is fast and retains volatile elements; dry ashing at 450 to 550 °C followed by dissolution in dilute nitric acid is cheaper but loses mercury entirely and partly loses arsenic, cadmium, lead and selenium by volatilisation and retention in silica. All glassware is acid-washed; reagent blanks are run with every batch.
4.4.2 Flame AAS (FAAS)

The sample solution is drawn by a pneumatic nebuliser into a spray chamber, where only the finest 5 to 10 percent of the aerosol reaches the burner; the rest drains to waste. An air-acetylene flame (about 2300 °C) through a 10 cm slot burner atomises most elements; the hotter nitrous oxide-acetylene flame (about 2900 °C) is needed for refractory, oxide-forming elements (aluminium, calcium at high concentration, silicon, titanium, vanadium). Atom residence time in the light path is only a few milliseconds. Consequences: detection limits in the mg/L (ppm) to high µg/L range (lead about 0.02 mg/L, cadmium about 0.002 mg/L), precision of 0.5 to 1 percent, analysis in 10 seconds per element, low cost, robust. Interferences: chemical (phosphate or sulfate forming refractory calcium compounds, overcome by adding lanthanum chloride as a releasing agent), ionisation (alkali and alkaline earth metals ionise in hot flames, suppressed by adding excess caesium or potassium), spectral (rare, because lines are narrow), and background absorption or scatter from salts (corrected by the deuterium lamp). FAAS is adequate for nutrients and additives (iron, zinc, copper, calcium, sodium, potassium in fortified foods, tin in canned foods at 250 mg/kg) but usually too insensitive for lead, cadmium and arsenic at the µg/kg limits now set for foods.
4.4.3 Graphite furnace AAS (GFAAS, electrothermal AAS, ETAAS)

A 10 to 50 µL aliquot is pipetted onto a L'vov platform inside a pyrolytically coated graphite tube, which is heated electrically under an argon purge (argon prevents the tube from burning) through a programme: drying at 100 to 120 °C (30 seconds) to evaporate solvent; pyrolysis or ashing at 400 to 1200 °C to destroy organic matter and volatilise matrix salts without losing the analyte; atomisation at 1800 to 2800 °C within 1 to 2 seconds, with gas flow stopped so the atom cloud is confined in the light path; and a clean-out step at 2600 °C. Matrix modifiers are added to allow a higher pyrolysis temperature: palladium with magnesium nitrate stabilises arsenic, selenium and lead; ammonium dihydrogen phosphate converts volatile cadmium and lead chlorides to less volatile phosphates. Because the entire sample is atomised into a confined volume and atoms reside for seconds rather than milliseconds, sensitivity improves 100 to 1000 fold: detection limits of 0.01 to 1 µg/L (ppb), for example lead 0.05 µg/L and cadmium 0.002 µg/L. Drawbacks: slow (2 to 3 minutes per determination, single element), strong background from matrix smoke requiring Zeeman correction, more chemical interference, higher cost, limited linear range, and need for the stabilised temperature platform furnace (STPF) protocol for reliable results. GFAAS is the workhorse for lead, cadmium and chromium in FSSAI contaminant testing where ICP-MS is unavailable.

blocks.text: 4.4.4 Hydride generation AAS (HGAAS)

Arsenic, selenium, antimony, bismuth, tellurium, tin and germanium have resonance lines in the far ultraviolet (arsenic 193.7 nm, selenium 196.0 nm) where the flame itself absorbs strongly, so direct FAAS is insensitive. These elements form volatile covalent hydrides when their lower oxidation states are reduced by sodium borohydride in hydrochloric acid:
NaBH4 + 3H2O + HCl → H3BO3 + NaCl + 8H (nascent hydrogen)
As3+ + 3H → AsH3 (arsine); Se4+ + 4H → SeH2 (hydrogen selenide); Sb3+ + 3H → SbH3 (stibine)

The gaseous hydride is swept by argon from the reaction vessel (or a continuous-flow manifold with a gas-liquid separator) into a quartz tube held at 900 to 1000 °C in the light path, where it decomposes to free atoms (2AsH3 → 2As + 3H2). Because the analyte is separated from the digest matrix and introduced as a gas with near 100 percent efficiency, sensitivity improves 10 to 100 fold over FAAS, with detection limits of 0.01 to 0.1 µg/L. Two chemistry points are routinely examined: the analyte must be in the lower oxidation state, so arsenic(V) is pre-reduced to arsenic(III) with potassium iodide and ascorbic acid, and selenium(VI) is pre-reduced to selenium(IV) by heating in 6 M hydrochloric acid; and transition metals (copper, nickel) interfere by consuming borohydride or decomposing the hydride, controlled by masking agents or dilution. HGAAS after digestion gives total inorganic arsenic; it does not respond to arsenobetaine, the dominant and non-toxic arsenic form in fish and shrimp, so a low HGAAS result on seafood is not a contradiction of a high total arsenic by ICP-MS. Arsenic speciation (arsenite, arsenate, methylated forms) requires HPLC coupled to ICP-MS and is relevant for rice, where FSSAI and Codex limit inorganic arsenic (Codex 0.2 mg/kg in polished rice, 0.35 mg/kg in husked rice) and drinking water is limited to 0.01 mg/L under IS 10500.
4.4.5 Cold vapour AAS (CVAAS) for mercury

Mercury is unique among metals in having an appreciable vapour pressure of the free monatomic element at room temperature, so no flame or furnace is required. After oxidative digestion (nitric and sulfuric acids with potassium permanganate or persulfate, in closed vessels to prevent loss, with excess oxidant destroyed by hydroxylamine hydrochloride just before measurement), mercury(II) is reduced to the metal with acidic stannous chloride:
Hg2+ + Sn2+ → Hg0 + Sn4+ (alternatively with sodium borohydride: Hg2+ + 2BH4- + 6H2O → Hg0 + 2H3BO3 + 7H2)

A stream of argon or air sweeps the mercury vapour through a drying tube into a long-path quartz absorption cell at room temperature, where absorbance is measured at the 253.7 nm resonance line from a mercury hollow cathode or electrodeless discharge lamp. Detection limits are 0.01 to 0.1 µg/L, improved a further 10 to 100 fold by pre-concentrating the vapour on a gold trap (amalgamation) and releasing it by heating. Cold vapour atomic fluorescence (CVAFS) is even more sensitive. Precautions: mercury adsorbs on surfaces and is lost on dry ashing or open-vessel heating; samples with high chloride can lose mercury as volatile chlorides; the technique measures total mercury, while the toxicologically relevant species in fish is methylmercury (about 90 percent of fish mercury, determined by GC-ECD, GC-AFS or LC-ICP-MS). FSSAI limits mercury in fish and fishery products at 0.5 mg/kg (1.0 mg/kg in listed predatory fish such as tuna, shark and swordfish) and methylmercury at 0.25 mg/kg, and mercury in other foods at 1.0 mg/kg under the Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations, 2011, as amended.
4.4.6 Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS)
Components and mechanism:

Sample introduction: a peristaltic pump feeds the digested solution (total dissolved solids kept below 0.2 percent) to a concentric or cross-flow nebuliser; a spray chamber passes only the finest aerosol (1 to 2 percent) to the plasma.

Torch and plasma: three concentric quartz tubes carry argon as plasma (outer, cooling) gas at 12 to 17 L per minute, auxiliary gas and nebuliser gas. A two- or three-turn copper load coil around the torch is driven by a radio-frequency generator at 27.12 MHz (some instruments use 40.68 MHz) at 1.0 to 1.6 kW. A Tesla spark seeds free electrons; the oscillating magnetic field accelerates them, their collisions ionise argon, and the resulting eddy currents sustain a self-heating, electrodeless plasma at 6000 to 10000 K (the analytical zone is about 6500 to 8000 K). The aerosol is desolvated, vaporised, atomised and ionised within a few milliseconds. Because the first ionisation energy of argon is 15.76 eV, every element with a lower first ionisation energy is ionised efficiently, more than 90 percent for most metals; only helium, neon and fluorine are not ionised, and elements with high ionisation energies (arsenic 9.8 eV, mercury 10.4 eV, selenium 9.75 eV) are ionised 30 to 50 percent, which still allows ng/L detection.

Interface: the plasma, at atmospheric pressure, is sampled through a water-cooled nickel or platinum sampler cone (orifice about 1 mm) into a region at a few torr, then through a skimmer cone (orifice about 0.4 mm) into the high vacuum; the supersonic expansion freezes the ion population.

Ion optics and collision-reaction cell: electrostatic lenses focus the ions and remove photons and neutrals; a collision-reaction cell filled with helium (kinetic energy discrimination) or a reactive gas (hydrogen, ammonia, oxygen) removes polyatomic interferences formed from argon, water and acids.

Mass analyser and detector: a quadrupole scans the full mass range 2 to 260 in less than a second, so all elements are determined simultaneously (quasi-simultaneously by fast sequential scanning); high-resolution sector field and triple quadrupole ICP-MS/MS variants resolve the most difficult interferences. A dual-mode electron multiplier covers nine orders of magnitude, from ng/L to hundreds of mg/L.

Performance: detection limits of 0.001 to 0.1 µg/L (sub-ppt to ppt) for lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic, uranium and the rare earths; 70 or more elements in two to three minutes; isotope ratio measurement (lead isotopes for source attribution, enriched stable isotopes for bioavailability studies); and coupling to HPLC or GC for speciation (inorganic arsenic in rice, methylmercury in fish, chromium(VI)). Internal standards (rhodium, indium, bismuth, germanium) correct for drift and matrix suppression. Interferences the examiner expects you to name: isobaric overlaps (114Sn on 114Cd, 204Hg on 204Pb, corrected by equations or alternative isotopes 111Cd and 208Pb) and polyatomic ions (40Ar35Cl+ on 75As, the classic problem in high-chloride seafood digests; 40Ar12C+ on 52Cr; 40Ar16O+ on 56Fe; 40Ar40Ar+ on 80Se; 35Cl16O+ on 51V), removed by the collision cell or by using hydrogen as reaction gas. Mercury shows a memory effect from adsorption in the sample path, controlled by adding gold (which forms a soluble mercury-gold complex) to all solutions. Limitations: capital and running cost (argon consumption about 15 to 20 L per minute), dissolved solids limit, the need for clean-room practices because the sensitivity makes laboratory contamination the dominant error. For comparison, ICP optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) uses the same plasma but measures emitted light, with detection limits in the µg/L range, suited to nutrient minerals rather than ultra-trace contaminants.

Part 5. Proximate Analysis (AOAC/FSSAI Methods)
PART 5: OFFICIAL PROXIMATE ANALYSIS PROTOCOLS (AOAC AND FSSAI MANUAL METHODS)
5.0 The Weende system

Proximate analysis, developed at the Weende Experiment Station (Henneberg and Stohmann, 1860s), partitions a food into six fractions: moisture, crude protein, crude fat (ether extract), total ash, crude fibre, and nitrogen-free extract (NFE, the digestible carbohydrate estimated by difference). The word crude signals that each fraction is defined by the method, not by chemistry: crude protein is nitrogen times a factor, crude fat is whatever the solvent dissolves, crude fibre is whatever survives acid and alkali. These are the methods cited in the FSSAI Manual of Methods of Analysis of Foods and in AOAC Official Methods, and they underpin nutrition labelling under the Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020, as well as standards of identity (for example minimum protein in milk powder, maximum moisture in spices and cereals).
NFE (percent) = 100 − (moisture + crude protein + crude fat + total ash + crude fibre), so every error in the five measured fractions accumulates in NFE.
5.1 Moisture

Moisture controls microbial stability (through water activity), texture, economic value (water sold at the price of food) and compliance with standards (for example not more than 14 percent in wheat flour, 12 percent in most spice powders, 5 percent in milk powder).
