5.2 Crude protein: the Kjeldahl method

Introduced by Johan Kjeldahl at the Carlsberg Laboratory (1883) and still the AOAC reference method (AOAC 955.04, 991.20 for milk, 2001.11; IS 7219). It measures total nitrogen (organic nitrogen plus ammonium, but not nitrate, nitrite, azo or nitro nitrogen without modification) and converts it to protein by a factor.
Step 1: Digestion (oxidation of organic matter and conversion of nitrogen to ammonium sulfate)

About 1 g of sample is heated with 15 to 25 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid, 10 to 15 g of potassium sulfate and a catalyst (0.3 to 1 g of copper sulfate, or copper with titanium dioxide, or selenium; mercuric oxide was the original catalyst but is now avoided for toxicity and because it binds ammonia, needing thiosulfate release) in a long-necked Kjeldahl flask or block digester at 380 to 420 °C for 1 to 3 hours, until the black charred liquid becomes clear and pale blue-green.
Organic nitrogen (in protein, R-NH2) + H2SO4 (with catalyst, heat) → (NH4)2SO4 + CO2 + SO2 + H2O

Roles of the reagents: sulfuric acid oxidises carbon and hydrogen and converts amino nitrogen to ammonium; potassium sulfate raises the boiling point of the acid from about 338 °C to about 380 to 400 °C, speeding digestion (too much salt and the temperature exceeds 410 °C, at which ammonia is lost); the copper catalyst accelerates oxidation of refractory nitrogen compounds (heterocyclic nitrogen in tryptophan, histidine, nicotinic acid digests slowly and incompletely without it).
Step 2: Neutralisation and steam distillation (liberation of ammonia)

The cooled digest is diluted with water and made strongly alkaline with 40 to 50 percent sodium hydroxide (excess, since the acid must be fully neutralised and the ammonium converted to free ammonia), then steam distilled.
(NH4)2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2NH3 (gas) + 2H2O

The ammonia is absorbed in a receiving flask containing 4 percent boric acid (about 25 to 50 mL) with a mixed indicator (methyl red and bromocresol green, or methyl red and methylene blue). Ammonia forms the ammonium-borate ion pair:
NH3 + H3BO3 → NH4+ + H2BO3−

The indicator turns from pinkish-red (acid) to green as ammonia is absorbed. Boric acid is a weak acid (pKa 9.2) that holds the ammonia but does not itself consume the titrant, which is the elegance of the method: no standardised receiving acid is needed and there is no back-titration. The older alternative collects ammonia in a measured excess of standard sulfuric or hydrochloric acid and back-titrates the unreacted acid with standard sodium hydroxide.
Step 3: Titration
The borate formed is titrated with standard 0.1 N hydrochloric acid (or sulfuric acid) until the indicator returns from green to the original pink end point:
H2BO3− + H+ (from HCl) → H3BO3
One mole of hydrochloric acid corresponds to one mole of ammonia and therefore to one mole of nitrogen (14.007 g).
Calculation
Nitrogen (percent) = [(V sample − V blank) × N × 1.4007] ÷ W
where V is the titre in mL, N the normality of the acid, 1.4007 the milliequivalent weight of nitrogen (14.007) multiplied by 100 and divided by 1000, and W the sample weight in grams.
Crude protein (percent) = Nitrogen (percent) × F

Worked example: 1.000 g of wheat flour, titre 10.50 mL of 0.1 N HCl, blank 0.20 mL. Nitrogen = (10.50 − 0.20) × 0.1 × 1.4007 ÷ 1.000 = 1.443 percent. Protein with the general factor = 1.443 × 6.25 = 9.02 percent; with the wheat factor = 1.443 × 5.70 = 8.22 percent. The difference of 0.8 percentage points is why FSSAI standards specify the factor.

Any nitrogen source raises the apparent protein: urea (46.6 percent N), ammonium salts, and melamine (66.6 percent N), the adulterant of the 2008 Chinese infant formula and pet food scandals. 5.3 Crude fat: Soxhlet solvent extraction
Devised by Franz von Soxhlet (1879) for milk fat and adopted as AOAC 920.39 (cereals), 960.39 (meat), 948.22 (nuts); IS 4684.
Apparatus and operation

The apparatus has three parts: a boiling flask containing the solvent, a central extraction chamber holding a cellulose thimble with 2 to 5 g of dried, finely ground sample (plugged with fat-free cotton), and a reflux condenser above. Solvent vapour rises through the side tube, condenses and drips onto the sample; the chamber fills with solvent, dissolving lipid; when the liquid reaches the top of the siphon arm, the entire contents siphon back into the flask. Each cycle (5 to 6 per hour) bathes the sample in fresh, distilled solvent, while the dissolved fat accumulates in the flask. This semi-continuous extraction runs for 6 to 16 hours (4 hours at 5 to 6 drops per second for most foods). The solvent is then recovered by distillation, the flask dried at 100 to 105 °C for 1 hour, cooled in a desiccator and weighed.
Crude fat (percent) = [(W flask with fat − W empty flask) ÷ W sample] × 100
Solvent choice

The sample must be dried first (moisture blocks penetration of the non-polar solvent and water would be co-extracted) and finely ground to expose lipid; cereals and oilseeds are usually ground to pass a 1 mm sieve.

Soxhlet measures free lipid only. Bound lipids in bakery products, dairy products and processed foods (lipoproteins, starch-lipid complexes, fat enclosed in intact cells) are released by acid hydrolysis before extraction (Weibull-Stoldt, AOAC 922.06: boiling with 3 N hydrochloric acid, filtering, drying, then Soxhlet), or by the Rose-Gottlieb alkaline (ammonia) ethanol-ether method for milk and infant formula (AOAC 905.02, Mojonnier flask), or the Gerber butyrometer method for milk (sulfuric acid digests protein, amyl alcohol aids separation, centrifugation reads fat directly; the field method of the Food Safety Officer).
Automated Soxtec (submersion then rinsing) and accelerated solvent extraction reduce time to under one hour.
Thermally labile lipids can oxidise during long extraction; the result is reported as crude fat or ether extract, never as triglyceride content.
5.4 Total ash and acid-insoluble ash
Total ash (dry ashing, AOAC 923.03, 942.05; IS 1155)

Ash is the inorganic residue after complete combustion of organic matter and is a measure of total mineral content (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, iron, trace metals present as oxides, carbonates, phosphates, chlorides, sulfates). Procedure: 2 to 5 g of sample in a tared silica, porcelain or platinum crucible is first charred gently over a flame or hot plate until smoking ceases (to prevent loss by spattering and foaming), then ignited in a muffle furnace at 550 °C (a range of 525 to 600 °C is specified by different methods) for 4 to 6 hours or overnight, until the ash is white or light grey and free of carbon. The crucible is cooled in a desiccator and weighed to constant weight.
Total ash (percent) = [(W crucible with ash − W empty crucible) ÷ W sample] × 100

Why 550 °C: high enough to burn carbon completely within hours, low enough to limit volatilisation of chlorides, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and of mercury, arsenic, selenium, cadmium and lead, and to limit fusion of the ash with the crucible. Black specks of unburnt carbon are treated by wetting the ash with water or dilute nitric acid, drying and re-ashing. Where sodium chloride is high (pickles, butter), 500 °C is used. Wet ashing (nitric, sulfuric and perchloric acids) and microwave digestion are preferred when the ash is to be analysed for individual metals (Part 4B). Sulfated ash (treatment with sulfuric acid before ignition, converting all cations to stable sulfates) is used for food additives and colours.
Acid-insoluble ash (AIA)

The total ash is boiled with 25 mL of dilute hydrochloric acid (about 10 percent, 1 part concentrated acid to 2.5 parts water) for 5 minutes; the soluble mineral salts dissolve, the solution is filtered through ashless filter paper, the residue is washed free of chloride with hot water, and the paper with residue is ignited again at 550 °C and weighed. The acid-insoluble ash is almost entirely silica: sand, soil, dust and grit. It is the statutory index of extraneous mineral adulteration in spices, flours and tea, and of poor washing of grains.

5.5 Crude fibre: the Weende method

Crude fibre is the organic residue that resists sequential boiling in dilute acid (simulating gastric digestion) and dilute alkali (simulating intestinal digestion) and is then lost on ignition (AOAC 962.09, 978.10; IS 10226).
Procedure
Weigh about 2 g of dried, fat-free sample (the Soxhlet residue is ideal; fat above 1 percent must be removed or it coats particles and interferes).

Acid digestion: boil gently with 200 mL of 1.25 percent (0.255 N) sulfuric acid under reflux for exactly 30 minutes, keeping the volume constant with hot water; filter through a linen cloth, Buchner funnel or fritted crucible, and wash with boiling water until the washings are no longer acid.

Alkali digestion: transfer the residue to 200 mL of 1.25 percent (0.313 N) sodium hydroxide and boil for exactly 30 minutes; filter and wash with boiling water until free of alkali, then with 25 mL of 1.25 percent sulfuric acid, three times with water, and finally with 25 mL of ethanol (and petroleum ether if fat remains).
Dry the residue in a crucible at 130 °C for 2 hours (or 100 to 105 °C overnight), cool in a desiccator and weigh (W1).
Ignite in a muffle furnace at 550 °C for 30 minutes (or until carbon free), cool and weigh (W2).
Crude fibre (percent) = [(W1 − W2) ÷ W sample] × 100

The loss on ignition is the crude fibre; the ash remaining (W2) is subtracted so that mineral matter trapped in the residue is not counted as fibre. Exact timing, acid and alkali concentrations and boiling intensity must be standardised because the result is purely operational.
What crude fibre is and is not

Crude fibre recovers 50 to 80 percent of the cellulose, only 10 to 50 percent of the lignin and under 20 percent of the hemicellulose, and none of the pectins, gums, beta-glucans or resistant starch; it therefore underestimates total dietary fibre by a factor of 2 to 5, and the ratio varies with the food. Crude fibre remains a legal standard of identity for spices, flours and animal feeds (for example FSSAI maximum crude fibre values in chilli powder and coriander powder, bran content in atta), but the nutrition label value for dietary fibre must come from the enzymatic-gravimetric method (AOAC 985.29 or 991.43, the Prosky method: digestion with heat-stable alpha-amylase, protease and amyloglucosidase, precipitation of soluble fibre with four volumes of ethanol, weighing of the residue corrected for its protein and ash) or AOAC 2009.01 and 2011.25 for total dietary fibre including resistant starch and low-molecular-weight oligosaccharides. For feeds, the Van Soest detergent system (neutral detergent fibre, acid detergent fibre, acid detergent lignin) is used.

Question 1: Packaging polymers and retort pouches
Consider the following statements:
High-density polyethylene has a lower density but a higher degree of crystallinity than low-density polyethylene, which is why it is a better moisture barrier.

In a four-ply retort pouch the biaxially oriented nylon (OPA) layer is positioned between the aluminium foil and the inner cast polypropylene sealant layer to provide puncture and flex-crack resistance.
Ethylene vinyl alcohol copolymer retains its exceptional oxygen barrier at all relative humidities and is therefore used as a monolayer retort film.

How many of the above statements are correct?
(a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None
Step-by-step verification:

Statement 1: HDPE has higher crystallinity (70 to 90 percent versus 40 to 50 percent) and therefore higher density (0.941 to 0.965 g/cm³ versus 0.910 to 0.925 g/cm³), not lower; the barrier conclusion is right but the density clause is wrong, so the statement as a whole is wrong. c1 = 0.
Statement 2: The four-ply construction is PET (12 µm) / aluminium foil (9 to 12 µm) / OPA (15 µm) / CPP (70 to 100 µm); nylon sits between foil and sealant to protect the foil from cracking. c2 = 1.

Statement 3: EVOH is hygroscopic; above about 75 percent RH its oxygen transmission rate rises ten to a hundred fold and it suffers retort shock; it is always buried as a core layer between polyolefin skins and never used as a monolayer. The absolute qualifier at all relative humidities is the trap. c3 = 0.
N = c1 + c2 + c3 = 0 + 1 + 0 = 1. Answer: (a) Only one.
Question 2: Active and intelligent packaging systems
Consider the following statements:
A methylene blue oxygen indicator inside a pack is pink in the absence of oxygen and turns blue when oxygen enters through a leaking seal.
A potassium permanganate ethylene absorber changes colour from purple to brown as permanganate is reduced to manganese dioxide, indicating exhaustion.
A polymerisation-based time-temperature indicator such as the Lifelines Fresh-Check label is classified as active packaging because it reacts chemically with temperature.

How many of the above statements are correct?
(a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None
Step-by-step verification:
Statement 1: In the reduced (leuco) state in an oxygen-free pack the tablet is pink; oxygen re-oxidises methylene blue to its blue form. c1 = 1.
Statement 2: KMnO4 (purple) oxidises ethylene and is itself reduced to MnO2 (brown); the colour change signals that capacity is spent. c2 = 1.

Statement 3: A TTI monitors and communicates the temperature history; it does not act on the food or the headspace, so it is intelligent packaging regardless of the chemistry inside the label. The reasoning (reacts chemically) is a distractor. c3 = 0.
N = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2. Answer: (b) Only two.
Question 3: FSSAI migration regulations
Consider the following statements with reference to the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations, 2018:
The overall migration limit for plastic food contact materials is 60 mg/kg of food or simulant, equivalently 10 mg/dm² of contact surface.
Food simulant B, 3 percent (w/v) acetic acid in water, represents acidic aqueous foods with a pH below 4.5 such as fruit juices, pickles and tomato products.
Newspapers and similar printed materials are prohibited for storing, wrapping or packaging food.

How many of the above statements are correct?
(a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None
Step-by-step verification:

Statement 1: Schedule IV sets the overall migration limit at 60 mg/kg or 10 mg/dm², identical to EU Regulation 10/2011; the two figures are linked by the convention of 6 dm² of packaging per kilogram of food (10 × 6 = 60). c1 = 1.
Statement 2: Simulant B is the only acidic simulant, 3 percent acetic acid, assigned to foods below pH 4.5. c2 = 1.

Statement 3: Regulation 4 of the 2018 Regulations prohibits newspaper and similar materials for storing and wrapping food, and also requires that the printed surface of any packaging must not come into direct contact with food; FSSAI had issued the same advisory in 2016. c3 = 1.
N = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. Answer: (c) All three.
Question 4: Instrumental analysis and proximate methods
Consider the following statements:
Flame atomic absorption spectrometry achieves lower (better) detection limits than graphite furnace atomic absorption spectrometry because the flame atomises the whole sample continuously.
The Kjeldahl nitrogen-to-protein conversion factor for milk and milk products is 5.70.
The electron capture detector gives a response proportional to the number of carbon atoms in every organic compound and is therefore the universal detector for gas chromatography.

How many of the above statements are correct?
(a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None
Step-by-step verification:

Statement 1: The reverse is true: the flame wastes 90 to 95 percent of the sample in the spray chamber and atoms reside only milliseconds in the beam, so FAAS works at mg/L; the graphite furnace atomises the whole 10 to 50 µL aliquot into a confined volume and reaches µg/L, 100 to 1000 times better. c1 = 0.
Statement 2: The milk factor is 6.38 (15.67 percent nitrogen in milk proteins); 5.70 is the wheat factor. c2 = 0.

Statement 3: Equal-carbon response and universality describe the flame ionisation detector; the electron capture detector with its 63Ni beta source responds selectively to electronegative, chiefly halogenated, compounds and barely responds to hydrocarbons. c3 = 0.
N = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0. Answer: (d) None.

Aluminium foil is always a 100 percent barrier. False: below 15 µm pinholes make it a barrier only within a laminate.

All recycled plastics are banned for food contact in India. False: certified food-grade recycled PET from approved recyclers is permitted after the amendment framework that followed the 2018 Regulations.
Passing the overall migration test proves the material is toxicologically safe. False: specific migration limits must also be met.
Mercury is determined by hydride generation AAS. False: cold vapour AAS at 253.7 nm.
Only Simulant E is a solid. True: Tenax, poly(2,6-diphenyl-p-phenylene oxide), for dry foods.
C-enamel is never used for acid fruit packs. True: zinc oxide would be extracted; R-enamel or plain heavy-tin cans are used.
The refractive index detector can be used with gradient elution. False.
Crude fibre never equals dietary fibre. True in practice: crude fibre underestimates dietary fibre by a factor of 2 to 5.

Question: Explain the architecture, material composition, and advantages of retort pouches over conventional tinplate cans in food preservation.

Suggested marking scheme: definition and context 1 mark; layer-by-layer architecture with gauges and functions 3 marks; heat-penetration mechanism 2 marks; comparative advantages 2 marks; limitations and process requirements 1 mark; regulatory and quality-control linkage 1 mark. Target length: 400 to 450 words, one labelled schematic, one table.
Model answer
Definition and context

A retort pouch is a flexible, heat-sealable, hermetically closed laminate container that withstands thermal sterilisation at 115 to 135 °C (typically 121 °C for 20 to 40 minutes, delivering the required F0 value) so that low-acid foods become commercially sterile and shelf stable at ambient temperature. It was developed by the United States Army Natick Laboratories with Reynolds Metals and Continental Flexible Packaging in the 1960s and 1970s for military rations and is now used for ready-to-eat curries, rice, tuna, soups and pet food. It is the flexible-packaging alternative to the three-piece tinplate can developed from Appert and Durand (1810).
Architecture and material composition
Schematic (outside to inside, food contact at the bottom):

rows: Reverse-printable surface, tensile and abrasion strength, heat resistance against sealing jaws

Essentially total barrier to oxygen, water vapour, light and aroma once laminated (foil below 15 µm has pinholes on its own, bridged by the adjacent polymer layers); provides 18 to 36 months shelf life
Puncture, flex-crack and abuse resistance; protects the foil in bony or sharp products
Cast polypropylene (CPP), often ethylene-modified random copolymer, 70 to 100 µm
Food-contact layer; heat seals at about 160 °C, survives 121 to 135 °C without delamination or seal loss, inert and low taint; thick enough to bridge seal-area contamination

blocks.text: The three-ply pouch is PET / Al / CPP; the four-ply pouch is PET / Al / OPA / CPP. Layers are bonded by two-component polyurethane adhesives that must be fully cured before use to prevent migration of primary aromatic amines. Transparent, microwaveable variants replace foil with PET-SiOx, PET-AlOx or EVOH barrier layers at some sacrifice of shelf life.
Heat-penetration mechanism

Sterilisation of conduction-heating foods is unsteady-state conduction, and the time for the cold spot to reach process temperature scales with the square of the conduction distance. A 307 × 409 can has a cold-spot path of about 36 mm, whereas a filled pouch is a slab 15 to 25 mm thick with a half-thickness of 8 to 12 mm. The pouch therefore reaches the same F0 in 30 to 50 percent less time at the same retort temperature, and because the entire slab heats almost uniformly the surface layers are not overcooked while the centre catches up.
Advantages over the tinplate can

rows: 30 to 50 percent shorter; less steam, water and cooling
Better retention of thiamine, vitamin C, colour, texture, flavour
Light; flat when empty, saving about 85 percent storage space
Tear-notch opening, boil-in-bag and microwave reheating (foil-free types)
Tin and iron pickup in plain cans (FSSAI tin limit 250 mg/kg); lacquer migration (bisphenol A from epoxy coatings)
Lower mass, but multilayer laminate is hard to recycle

blocks.text: Limitations and process requirements

The pouch must be processed in an overpressure retort (steam-air or water immersion) because internal vapour pressure at 121 °C would otherwise burst seals; pouches are racked flat to control thickness; residual air must be kept below about 10 mL by vacuum or steam-flush sealing; seals must be clean and are tested for strength, burst pressure and leaks; filling is slower and unit cost higher than canning; and the pouch needs a carton for distribution.
Regulatory linkage

The laminate materials must conform to Schedule IV of the FSS (Packaging) Regulations, 2018 (overall migration not more than 60 mg/kg or 10 mg/dm² by IS 9845, and specific migration limits for metals and DEHP), and the product must meet FSSAI commercial sterility requirements, verified by incubation at 37 °C for 10 days (and 55 °C for thermophiles). The Food Safety Officer inspects seal integrity, residual air, retort records (F0, come-up time, overpressure) and incubation results.
Conclusion: the retort pouch delivers can-equivalent sterility with a thinner geometry, giving faster, gentler processing and higher product quality, at the cost of stricter seal and process control.
15-Mark Model Answer

Question: Examine the statutory framework of Food Packaging under FSSAI Regulations (2018). Detail the food simulants used for migration testing, the difference between overall and specific migration limits, and the statutory prohibitions on packaging materials.

Suggested marking scheme: legal basis and structure of the Regulations 3 marks; general requirements 2 marks; food simulants with compositions and food classes 3 marks; overall versus specific migration with the statutory numbers 3 marks; prohibitions 2 marks; enforcement, testing and conclusion 2 marks. Target length: 650 to 750 words, two tables, one callout for the number link.
Model answer
Legal basis and structure

Section 92 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 empowers the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India to make regulations, and Section 16 charges it with specifying standards for packaging. The Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations, 2018 were notified on 24 December 2018 and came into force on 1 July 2019, separating packaging from the earlier combined Packaging and Labelling Regulations, 2011 (labelling now sits in the Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020). The Regulations contain general requirements, specific requirements, and schedules: Schedule I (paper and board), Schedule II (glass), Schedule III (metals and alloys: tinplate, tin-free steel, aluminium, stainless steel), Schedule IV (plastics, with overall and specific migration limits and the Indian Standards for each polymer, for example IS 10146 polyethylene, IS 10910 polypropylene, IS 12252 PET, IS 10151 PVC, IS 12247 nylon, IS 13601 polycarbonate), and an indicative list of suggested packaging materials for food categories (dairy, fats and oils, cereals, meat and fish, fruits and vegetables, beverages, water, spices). The Regulations are to be read with the Contaminants, Toxins and Residues Regulations (limits for metals and migrants in food) and with the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016.
General requirements

Packaging materials must be of food grade and must not transfer their constituents to food in quantities that could endanger human health, change the composition of the food unacceptably, or deteriorate its organoleptic properties (the inertness principle shared with EU Regulation 1935/2004).
Materials must conform to the Indian Standards listed in the Schedules; the food business operator must obtain a certificate of conformity from an NABL-accredited laboratory.
Packaging must be suitable for the type of food and its storage and processing conditions (hot fill, retort, frozen, microwave).
Pigments and colourants in plastics must comply with IS 9833; the printed surface must not contact food.
Containers must be free of defects: no rust, improper seaming, dents or leakage in cans; glass free of flaws that could cause breakage; paper free of harmful dyes and loading materials.
Food simulants for migration testing

Foods are too variable to test directly, so standardised liquids and solids that mimic the extractive power of food classes are used (EU Regulation 10/2011 Annex III; the same logic underlies IS 9845 referenced by Schedule IV).

Alcoholic foods above 20 percent; oil-in-water emulsions; milk and dairy products

blocks.text: The two overall figures express one ceiling: regulators assume a 60 kg adult eats 1 kg of food per day that contacted 6 dm² of packaging (a 1 litre cube has 6 dm² of surface), so 10 mg/dm² × 6 dm²/kg = 60 mg/kg. The surface-based figure is applied to sheet materials and small containers; the mass-based figure to larger containers. Passing the overall test does not prove safety: a material can be under 60 mg/kg overall and still exceed the SML of a potent migrant such as bisphenol A or a primary aromatic amine, so both tests are required. Where a syllabus source quotes lead at 1 mg/kg, write the Schedule IV value (0.01 mg/kg) and note that 1 mg/kg is the barium limit.
Statutory prohibitions

Newspaper and similar printed materials shall not be used for storing, wrapping or packaging food; printing inks carry lead, benzophenone, mineral oil hydrocarbons and primary aromatic amines, and the paper carries microbial load.
The printed surface of any packaging material shall not come into direct contact with food (reverse printing or an unprinted inner layer is required).

Recycled plastics shall not be used for packaging, storing, carrying or dispensing food, except that food-grade recycled PET produced by recyclers registered and certified under the subsequent FSSAI and Central Pollution Control Board framework (consistent with the amended Plastic Waste Management Rules) may be used for direct food contact; recycled paper and board bearing print or of unknown origin remain unsuitable for direct contact.

Plastics not listed with an Indian Standard in Schedule IV, and pigments or colourants outside IS 9833, are not permitted; non-food-grade, rusted, dented or previously used containers, and lead-soldered cans, are prohibited.
Packaging must not be used for a food category for which it is unsuitable (for example non-retortable films for sterilised products, or unlacquered cans for sulfur-rich foods).
Enforcement and testing linkage

The Food Safety Officer may draw samples of packaging along with food under Section 38 of the Act; overall migration is tested gravimetrically by IS 9845, metals by AAS or ICP-MS (lead and cadmium by graphite furnace or ICP-MS at 0.01 mg/kg), DEHP by GC-MS, bisphenol A by LC-MS/MS, and PET bottles for packaged drinking water must meet BIS requirements including acetaldehyde control. Non-conformity attracts penalties under Sections 50 to 66 for sub-standard, unsafe or misbranded food.

Conclusion: the 2018 Regulations convert the inertness principle into enforceable numbers (60 mg/kg or 10 mg/dm² overall; substance-specific SMLs), standardised simulants, Indian Standard conformity, and clear prohibitions (newspaper, printed contact surfaces, uncertified recycled plastics), while the certified food-grade recycled PET exception shows the framework evolving towards circular packaging without compromising migration safety.
